b:
Types: Universal eye speculum • Guarded eye speculum • Wire speculum.
Universal — Identification: It has a spring, two limbs and a screw to adjust the limbs. Called universal because it can be used on either side. Method: Fixed to the eyelids with the screw facing outward and forward. Uses: Separates both eyelids for good exposure of the eyeball, mainly in extraocular operations: pterygium excision, squint operation, evisceration and enucleation, debridement and cautery of corneal ulcer, subconjunctival / sub-Tenon's injection, removal of corneal foreign body, removal of conjunctival cyst or mass, suture removal. Disadvantages: (a) No guard, so the upper-lid lashes (larger) come into the field. (b) NOT used in intraocular operations — more vitreous upthrust and risk of vitreous loss from pressure on the globe.
Guarded — Identification: The upper limb has a guard plate which keeps the upper-lid lashes away from the field, so two instruments are required (right and left). Uses: Same as universal; specially useful in squint surgery in children and in pterygium surgery. Disadvantages: operating field reduced; heavier, so more pressure on the globe.
Wire speculum: Made of stainless-steel wire, no screw, universal. Very light, so little pressure on the eyeball — usable in BOTH intraocular and extraocular operations.
Do not confuse with Müller's retractor, which has 2–3 right-angle sharp-pointed pins (teeth) underneath to engage the skin flap.

Identification: Medium-size, fully serrated forceps with a catch; straight or curved — curved used more frequently. (Video: mosquito haemostat — blunt tips, transverse serrations, ratchet lock on the finger rings.)
Uses: (a) Hold lid stitches and the superior rectus stitch, fixing the suture ends to the head towel. (b) Crush the lateral canthus in lateral canthotomy. (c) Haemostasis during DCR/DCT, especially if the angular vein is damaged. (d) Fasanella–Servat operation for ptosis — clamps conjunctiva, tarsal plate, Müller's muscle and levator. (e) Hold the muscle stump during enucleation. (f) Make an irrigating cystitome from a 26-gauge disposable needle. (g) Hold the whole lacrimal sac before excision in DCT. Also clamping bleeding vessels in lid / lacrimal surgery.

Identification: Straight fine scissors with pointed tips; may be curved. (Video: corneal / conjunctival spring scissors, e.g. Westcott's, are spring-action with longer, thicker blades than Vannas.)
Uses: (a) Dissect the bulbar conjunctiva / peritomy and make the conjunctival flap in cataract, trabeculectomy, squint, retinal detachment and enucleation surgery. (b) Cut suture ends. (c) Cut other tissues — Tenon's capsule, pterygium, skin edges.
Conjunctival flap in cataract surgery: Limbal-based flap — conjunctiva cut a few mm away from the limbus and reflected over the cornea from its attached base at the limbus. Fornix-based flap — cut AT the limbus and retracted towards the fornix. Fornix-based flap is better than limbal-based flap.

Identification: Small curved spring scissors with sharp small blades. Called universal because it is used to cut both the right and left halves of the section (right half = temporal half of the right cornea and nasal half of the left cornea, and vice versa).
Uses: (a) Extend the ab-externo section in cataract surgery. (b) Cut the corneal button from donor and recipient eyes in keratoplasty. (c) Cut 8-0 suture ends. (d) Cut the iris for iridectomy.

Identification: Butterfly-shaped spring scissors with the cutting blades bent at an angle of 60° to the handle; two wings on the handle for index finger and thumb; one blade has a pointed tip, the other a rounded tip.
Method: Held so the plane of the blade lies in the same plane as the iris, with the handle almost vertical.
Uses: (a) Cut a piece of iris tissue in iridectomy. (b) Anterior / open-sky vitrectomy for vitreous loss during cataract extraction. (c) Cut trabecular tissue with part of the sclera in trabeculectomy. (d) Cut 8-0 / 10-0 suture ends. (e) During corneoscleral suturing.

Identification: A ring of wire (round or oval) at the end of a narrow limb attached to a handle, like a large platinum loop; may be slightly curved like a spoon.
Method: Pupil must be fully dilated. Never pass it blindly — the lens edge should be visible. Pass carefully behind the lens, lift the lens and take it out. Vitreous loss is inevitable in vectis delivery; sometimes a sector iridectomy is needed instead of a peripheral iridectomy; open-sky vitrectomy is done after lens delivery.
Uses: (a) Remove a subluxated or dislocated lens. (b) Deliver the nucleus in ECCE with an irrigating vectis; in SICS/ECCE it slides beneath the nucleus and extracts it while the posterior scleral lip is depressed.
If the vectis is not available: the end of McNamara's spoon, or intracapsular forceps — closed tips passed carefully behind the lens, opened a little so the lens sits on them, then lifted out.

Identification: Medium-sized spring needle holder with two narrow, fine, curved jaws; available with or without a catch. The demonstrated one has NO lock, to prevent tissue jerking when the needle is released.
Uses: Catches fine needles (5-0, 6-0, 8-0 and 10-0 sutures) for: (a) corneoscleral suturing after cataract surgery; (b) scleral suturing in squint, detachment and trabeculectomy surgery; (c) corneal suturing in penetrating injury or keratoplasty; (d) suturing the mucosal flaps in DCR; (e) sometimes conjunctival suturing.

Identification: Much smaller scissors with spring action; straight, curved or angular.
Uses: (a) Prepare the conjunctival flap. (b) Cut 10-0 sutures in cataract or keratoplasty surgery. (c) Cut the trabecular flap in trabeculectomy. (d) Cut anterior capsular tags in ECCE / capsulotomy. (e) Cut vitreous in open-sky / anterior vitrectomy (vitreous loss in ICCE/ECCE, or after a posterior capsular rent). (f) Cut the corneal button after trephination in corneal grafting. (g) Cut iris in the different types of iridectomy; also sphincterotomy in a small, rigid pupil.

Identification: An angular fine hook attached to a long round solid handle, ending in a tiny blunt right-angled hook with no teeth.
Methods & uses: (a) Dial the IOL for centration and to bring the haptics into the horizontal position — the hook is placed in the dialling holes of the optic and rotated clockwise. (b) Left-hand (second) instrument in phacoemulsification: rotate the lens nucleus, crack the nucleus after quadrant trenching, chop the nucleus. (c) In SICS, prolapse the nucleus into the anterior chamber.

Identification: Forceps with a large screw for fixing/tightening the limbs like a clamp; one limb has a solid disc-shaped plate, the other a ring at its end. Haemostatic and self-retaining.
Method: The solid plate is applied on the skin surface of the lid and the ring on the tarsal conjunctiva, encircling the chalazion; the screw is tightened, the lid everted and the chalazion exposed for incision. Functions of the screw: fixation of the lid + haemostasis by tightening.
Uses: (a) Fix the chalazion for surgery and ensure haemostasis. (b) Intralesional steroid injection into a chalazion after fixing it. (c) Excision of a small granuloma or papilloma of the lid.
Pearl: the incision on the palpebral conjunctiva is VERTICAL, because the Meibomian glands run vertically in the tarsal plate — a horizontal incision would damage adjacent healthy ducts.

t: 11 · Punctum Dilator (Nettleship's) — with the method of syringing
b:
Identification: A long, narrow, solid cylindrical instrument with a smooth conical pointed tip; the body is corrugated for better grip with thumb and index finger.
Method of syringing: (a) Anaesthetise the eye with 4% lignocaine or 1% proparacaine drops. (b) Pull the lower lid and identify the lower punctum in bright light. (c) Hold the dilator vertically and place it on the punctal opening. (d) Twist with light pressure and introduce it into the punctum. (e) Then hold it horizontally and push medially by rotatory movement following the course of the canaliculus (first vertical, then horizontal); withdraw it. (f) Introduce the lacrimal cannula, fitted on a syringe filled with distilled water, in the same direction. (g) Push the piston and ask the patient whether water has reached the throat — or note the swallowing movement of the neck.
Uses: (a) Dilate the punctum and part of the canaliculus before syringing. (b) Dilate the punctum for probing in congenital dacryocystitis. (c) Dilate, then probe, to identify the lacrimal sac during DCR. (d) Dilatation in congenital or acquired punctal stenosis. (e) Before dacryocystography (DCG). (f) As a marker (tip dipped in gentian violet) in squint or retinal detachment surgery.

Identification: A measuring caliper in which the measurement (in mm) is adjusted by the spring action of a screw; ends pointed like a compass, scale fixed at the opposite end (0–20 mm). The exact measurement is read where the pointed end indicates on the scale.
Uses: Measure the size of the cornea (buphthalmos, megalocornea, microcornea, white-to-white for ACIOL sizing). In surgery: phacoemulsification / SICS — length of incision; trabeculectomy — length of scleral flap; squint surgery — amount of resection or recession; keratoplasty — size of donor and recipient corneal button; retinal detachment surgery — distance for passing the encircling band; IOFB removal — site of incision; ptosis surgery — amount of LPS to be resected; pars-plana intravitreal injections and vitrectomy ports — distance behind the limbus: 4.0 mm in phakic eyes, 3.5 mm in pseudophakic eyes, 3.0 mm in aphakic eyes; and measurement for any other purpose.

Identification: A cylindrical instrument with three parts: (a) a circular blade, (b) an adjustable inner core — the obturator, (c) a cover to protect the sharpness of the blade. Available in different diameters (6.0, 6.5, 7.0, 7.5, 10, 10.5 mm etc.). The obturator has a scale (markings in 1/10 mm) which helps the surgeon select the exact depth of cornea to be cut — important in lamellar keratoplasty.
Use: To cut the donor and recipient corneal button in penetrating and lamellar keratoplasty.

Dimensions: Optic 5–7 mm; haptic (overall diameter) about 12 mm.
Types by position: Anterior chamber IOL, posterior chamber IOL, iris-supported IOL.
By material: Rigid IOL — PMMA. Foldable IOL — silicone, acrylic, hydrogel, collamer. Rollable IOL — hydrogel.
Video notes: The foldable IOL cartridge and injector fold and inject a foldable IOL (acrylic — hydrophobic or hydrophilic, silicone, hydrogel) through a small incision (under 3 mm) into the capsular bag in phacoemulsification. The rigid (non-foldable) PMMA IOL has a central circular optic and two side haptics, which may have positioning / dialling holes, and is used in SICS and ECCE.
Power of IOL — SRK formula: P = A − 2.5L − 0.9K, where P = power of the IOL, A = constant specific for each lens type, L = axial length of the eyeball in mm, K = average corneal curvature.

Use: To verify the strength and the axis of the cylindrical lens in subjective refraction.
Commonly used powers: ±0.25 D and ±0.50 D.

What it is: Many glass rods of red colour set together in a metallic disc (a point of light viewed through it is seen as a line).
Uses: Macular function test; diplopia testing.

Use: Red–green goggles are used for diplopia charting.
Worth's four-dot test: The patient wears a red lens in front of the right eye and a green lens in front of the left eye and views a box with 4 lights — 1 red, 2 green and 1 white (interpretation — refer to Khurana).

Use: A vital dye injected into the anterior chamber (under an air bubble) to stain the anterior lens capsule blue during anterior capsulotomy / capsulorhexis, providing contrast — especially in mature white cataracts, where the red fundal glow is absent and the unstained capsule is nearly invisible.

Functions: (a) Maintain the anterior chamber — a space maintainer. (b) Protective coating in the anterior chamber in phacoemulsification. HPMC (hydroxypropyl methylcellulose 2%) is called a "soft surgical tool": it maintains AC depth and coats and protects the corneal endothelium from mechanical trauma during phaco / nucleus delivery and IOL insertion; sodium hyaluronate 1% / 1.4% is another cohesive viscoelastic used the same way.
Preparations: Methyl cellulose, sodium hyaluronate 1%, hypromellose 2%, chondroitin sulphate (20% and 50%). Alternatives: air, serum, balanced salt solution, other blood products.
Side effect: Post-operative rise in IOP if not washed out completely.
Uses: (a) Cataract surgery with or without IOL — maintain the AC, prevent entry of blood and fluid, protect the corneal endothelium, coat the IOL. (b) Glaucoma surgery. (c) Keratoplasty. (d) Retinal detachment surgery. (e) Repair of the globe in perforating injuries.

t: 20 · Iris Forceps, Method of Iridectomy & Types of Iridectomy
b:
Identification: A small lightweight forceps with 1:2 teeth on the inner side of its tips; if the limb is closed, the teeth cannot be seen or felt. The shape may be straight, curved or angular.
Method of iridectomy: (a) Hold it with the tips facing the 12 o'clock position, angled towards 6 o'clock. (b) Enter the AC with closed tips and touch the peripheral iris. (c) Open the forceps a little, catch a pinch of iris and take a triangular fold of iris out of the section. (d) Cut a small triangular piece radially with De Wecker's scissors. Always check the severed iris by rubbing it over the face mask — release of pigment means the iridectomy is full thickness.
Types of iridectomy: 1. Peripheral button-hole (at 11 and/or 1 o'clock; one full-thickness iridectomy is as effective as two) — in ICCE (prevents pupillary-block glaucoma and iris prolapse: aqueous flows into the AC through the bypass, keeping AC–PC equilibrium), angle-closure glaucoma, as part of trabeculectomy, and in penetrating keratoplasty. 2. Optical — central corneal opacity where keratoplasty is not available, rarely polar cataract; done in the LOWER part of the iris (the upper opening would be covered by the upper lid), site judged by the stenopaeic slit test at the clearest zone — down-and-in for literates, down-and-out for illiterates. 3. Glaucoma iridectomy / iridodialysis — in congestive glaucoma the iris is torn from its root instead of being cut. 4. Broad or complete — to facilitate lens extraction when the pupil is small and rigid, with extensive synechiae, or after vitreous loss; also for prolapsed iris, iris foreign body, tumour or cyst. 5. Preliminary — a test iridectomy in uveitis causing complicated cataract, done at the first sitting to see the reaction. 6. Involuntary — iris cut by the cataract knife during an ab-interno section when the AC is shallow. Note: YAG laser peripheral iridotomy is better in an acute attack of ACG — non-invasive (no infection risk) and a cheap OPD procedure.
Video — surgical PI vs laser iridotomy: Nd:YAG laser (1064 nm, photodisruption) is non-invasive; surgical PI excises peripheral iris with Colibri / iris forceps and Vannas / De Wecker's scissors. PI indications: primary angle-closure glaucoma (relieves pupillary block — maximal at a mid-dilated pupil of 4–5 mm, which traps aqueous and causes iris bombe — by opening a bypass from posterior to anterior chamber), prophylactic PI in the fellow eye after acute angle closure, part of trabeculectomy (so the iris does not plug the internal ostium), complicated cataract surgery (ACIOL / iris-claw lens, iris prolapse, shallow AC), excision of small iris tumours and removal of intracameral foreign bodies.

Identification: A thin straight blade with a sharp pointed tip and a cutting edge; the other edge is blunt. The blade may be thin or thick. It may have a sliding case arrangement keeping the sharp end covered to protect its tip when not in use.
Uses: (a) Ab-interno section in cataract surgery. (b) Optical iridectomy. (c) Paracentesis. (d) Glaucoma iridectomy. (e) Suture removal after cataract surgery. (f) Dissecting the head in pterygium surgery, or giving the incision in chalazion surgery. (g) 4-point iridotomy in iris bombe (quadripuncture).

Identification: A flat handle with a short grooved neck. Handle No. 3 is used in ophthalmic surgery; the fitted blades are No. 11 (triangular blade) or No. 15 (curved tip).
Uses: (a) Ab-externo corneoscleral section for cataract surgery. (b) Trabeculectomy. (c) Skin incision in DCR, ptosis and other lid surgeries. (d) Dissect the pterygium head from the cornea. (e) Incision in chalazion surgery. (f) Suture removal after cataract surgery.
Advantages in cataract surgery: It is a guarded section — slow release of aqueous, so the chance of quick decompression of the globe is almost nil; it is stepped (biplanar or triplanar), so wound security is better. Disadvantages: A conjunctival flap is usually necessary before the section; it is time-consuming.

Identification: An instrument to break a razor blade (must be carbon steel, e.g. the 'Bharat' blade). Medium size, with two jaw-like plates at the tip to catch the razor blade firmly; the other end has a catch for a better grip. At least 8 blade fragments can be made from a single razor blade.
Advantages: Cheaper than any other knife-blade, and sharper than No. 11 or No. 15. Disadvantage: Only breakable carbon-steel razor blades are used, so rust formation is a problem.
Uses: The same as the Bard-Parker knife. Instruments used for the corneoscleral section: cataract knife, Bard-Parker knife, blade breaker with razor blade, disposable super-blades, keratome, diamond knife.

Identification: An ordinary straight forceps without any teeth at its tips; the ends are a little blunt and their inner surface has fine serrations for a better grip.
Uses: (a) Hold the bulbar conjunctiva during its dissection. (b) Hold episcleral tissue during its dissection. (c) Suturing of the conjunctiva. (d) Hold the conjunctiva during subconjunctival injection. (e) Hold small sponge swabs.

Colibri (A) — Identification: A curved or angular forceps with fine limbs and 1:2 teeth at the tip; thicker and stout; named after the hummingbird; it also has a tying platform.
St. Martin's (B) — Identification: A straight, small but stout forceps with 1:2 teeth at its fine tip.
Uses (both): (a) Hold the cornea and scleral lips during corneoscleral suturing after cataract surgery, and the corneal lips in repair of penetrating injury or wound closure in keratoplasty. (b) Hold the scleral lip for dissection and scleral suturing (trabeculectomy). (c) Hold the corneal lip in cataract surgery to extend the section with a knife. (d) Lift the cornea upwards during application of the cryoprobe. (e) May be used in iridectomy — holding the iris for a peripheral iridectomy.

Identification: A stout forceps with double curvature (S-shaped) at its ends and 1:2 teeth at its tip; the curvature at the tip fits the curvature of the globe.
Use: Catches the superior rectus muscle belly — through the conjunctiva at 12 o'clock, about 7.7 mm behind the limbus — for passing stay (bridle) sutures, so the eyeball can be rotated and fixed downwards in cataract, glaucoma or other surgery, exposing the superior limbus and sclera. Also used to catch the inferior rectus, as in keratoplasty.

Identification: A small straight or curved forceps with long fine limbs; no teeth at the tip; the tips are made stout by an extra-thick platform.
Uses: (a) Hold the suture ends while tying the sutures after proper tightening. (b) Hold the cut ends of the suture during its removal. (c) Catch the margin of incised conjunctiva during suturing. (d) Remove caterpillar hair.

Identification: A fine, medium-sized toothless forceps with an angulation at about 7–8 mm from its tip and smooth, flat tying platforms; no lock.
Uses: (a) Hold the intraocular lens during its placement in the posterior chamber. (b) Catch and remove the loose anterior capsule after completion of capsulotomy. (c) Tying fine microsurgical sutures (10-0 nylon, 8-0 vicryl) in cataract surgery, trabeculectomy and corneal tear repair — a locking instrument is never used for delicate sutures, because unlocking causes a sudden jerk.

Identification: Two limbs with three curved pins on each side for engaging the edges of the skin incision; the limbs are kept in the retracted position with the help of a fixing screw.
Uses: To retract the skin (and orbicularis) and achieve haemostasis by compressing vessels during surgery on the lacrimal sac — DCT and DCR.

Identification: A flat, thin, diamond-shaped blade with a sharp apex and two cutting edges.
Uses: To make valvular corneal incisions for entry into the anterior chamber during all modern techniques of cataract extraction — phacoemulsification, SICS and even conventional ECCE — and other intraocular surgeries, e.g. iridectomy and paracentesis.
Sizes (video): 2.8 mm (or 2.2 mm) — the standard entry keratome for phacoemulsification (incisions under 3 mm) and the initial entry in SICS. 3.2 mm / 5.2 mm / 5.5 mm — extension keratomes used to enlarge the internal incision in SICS or for foldable / non-foldable IOL insertion.

Identification: A small lancet-shaped needle with sharp cutting edges, resembling a small keratome in appearance; it has a guard to prevent inadvertent injury to the deeper structures.
Uses: (a) For paracentesis. (b) To make very small corneoscleral incisions.

Identification: A fine straight knife with a sharp pointed tip and a cutting edge on one side — the 15-degree bevelled lance-tip knife.
Use: To make a small valvular clear-corneal incision (the side-port incision) at the limbus / clear cornea in phacoemulsification and other intraocular surgeries, including pars plana vitrectomy.
Uses of the side-port incision (video): During cataract surgery — injecting viscoelastic, trypan blue dye or intracameral drugs; introducing micro-instruments (cystitome / capsulotomy needle, Sinskey hook / chopper); cortical wash (irrigation and aspiration). As standalone paracentesis — hyphaema wash (blood and clots from the AC after trauma or surgery), and in CRAO (central retinal artery occlusion) an emergency paracentesis suddenly lowers IOP, helping dislodge the embolus to a more peripheral branch.

Identification: A fine, straight but triangular knife, similar to the 15° side-port entry blade but with cutting edges on BOTH sides.
Uses: Similar to the 15° side-port entry blade — small valvular clear-corneal incisions, including pars plana entry.

Identification: A blunt-tipped, bevel-up knife with a cut-splitting action at the tip and at both sides; the blade is curved and either mounted on a plastic handle (disposable) or fixed to a metallic handle.
Use: To make the tunnel incision in the sclera and cornea for phacoemulsification, manual SICS and sutureless trabeculectomy — dissecting the self-sealing triplanar sclerocorneal tunnel.

Identification: A D-shaped plate opposed by a U-shaped fenestrated rim, tightened with a screw (bandwheel). Two clamps are required — one can be used for the right lower and left upper lid, the second for the left lower and right upper lid; the handle is always on the temporal side. While applying it, the plate is kept towards the conjunctival side and the rim on the skin side.
Advantage over a lid spatula: It is self-retaining and does not need an assistant to hold it. Disadvantages: The operative field is less; pressure necrosis can occur if fitted tightly.
Uses: Lid surgery, e.g. entropion and ectropion correction — it protects the eyeball, supports the lid tissue and provides haemostasis during surgery.

Identification: Available in various designs — commonly Simcoe's classical or reverse (indirect) cannula, and a J-shaped variant. It is a two-way cannula: one port connects to an IV infusion line for continuous irrigation, the other to a 10 ml or 5 ml syringe via silicone tubing for manual aspiration.
Uses: (a) Irrigation and aspiration of the lens (cortical) matter in ECCE. (b) Aspiration of hyphaema; viscoelastic wash.
Video — I/A in phaco: Bimanual I/A uses two separate handpieces through two side ports — an irrigation handpiece with two side openings, and an aspiration handpiece with a single 0.3 mm opening at the tip for residual cortex (especially sub-incisional cortex). Coaxial I/A combines irrigation (outer silicone sleeve with two side ports) and aspiration (central metal tip) in one probe through the main corneal incision.

Identification: A spring-action forceps with short, blunt and curved blades having smooth edges and tips with a platform — no teeth or serrations.
Use: To hold the optic of a non-foldable PMMA IOL during implantation.

Identification: A small cup with sharp margins attached to a narrow handle.
Use: To scoop out the contents of the chalazion during incision and curettage.
What is a chalazion? A chronic, non-infectious lipogranulomatous inflammation of a Meibomian (tarsal) gland, presenting as a painless tarsal nodule.

Identification: A set of straight, malleable metal wires of varying thickness (sizes 0–8) with blunt rounded ends and a flattened central platform.
Uses: (a) To probe the nasolacrimal duct in congenital block — therapeutic probing in congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction when conservative Crigler massage has failed (usually after 6–12 months of age); also diagnostic probing in canalicular block. (b) To identify the lacrimal sac during DCT and DCR operations.

Identification: A stout spring handle and two blades attached at a right angle; the upper blade has a small hole with a sharp cutting edge and the lower blade has a cup-like depression.
Use: To enlarge the bony opening during DCR by punching the bone from the margins of the opening. Carelessness during this step can cause accidental damage to the nasal mucosa and the nasal septum.

t: 41 · Optic Nerve Guard (Wells Enucleation Spoon) & Enucleation
b:
Identification: A spoon-shaped instrument with a central cleavage (U-shaped slot). The enucleation scissors used with it are stout, strong and curved, with blunt tips.
Use: To engage and guard the optic nerve during enucleation — after peritomy and detaching all 6 extraocular muscles, the guide is slid behind the globe to engage the optic nerve, which is then severed with the enucleation scissors.
Indications for enucleation (video): (1) Intraocular malignant tumours — retinoblastoma in children (cut a LONG optic-nerve stump, 10–15 mm) and malignant melanoma of the choroid in adults; evisceration is contraindicated in tumours. (2) Painful blind eye — e.g. absolute glaucoma, neovascular glaucoma. (3) Severe perforating / crushing ocular trauma — badly mutilated globe with no visual potential (to prevent sympathetic ophthalmitis in the fellow eye). (4) Phthisis bulbi or non-bleeding anterior staphyloma, for cosmetic fitting of an ocular prosthesis.

Identification: A small but stout rectangular blade with a slightly convex surface and a blunt edge, attached to a handle (a shallow oval / rectangular metallic scoop).
Use: To separate out the uveal tissue from the sclera and scoop out all the inner contents of the globe (lens, vitreous, retina and uveal tract) during evisceration, leaving the outer scleral shell and extraocular muscles intact. All uveal pigment must be thoroughly scraped off the sclera to prevent sympathetic ophthalmitis.
Indications for evisceration (video): (1) Panophthalmitis — severe purulent inflammation of the whole globe including Tenon's capsule. Enucleation is strictly contraindicated here, because cutting the optic nerve opens the subarachnoid meningeal sheaths and can spread infection to the brain (meningitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis); a frill excision leaves a small collar of sclera around the optic nerve for drainage. (2) Expulsive choroidal haemorrhage. (3) Bleeding anterior staphyloma.
Viva distinction — atrophic bulbi vs phthisis bulbi: Atrophic bulbi — shrunken, non-functional eye with internal tissue organisation still preserved, quadrilateral (square) in shape from the pull of the four rectus muscles on the hypotonic globe. Phthisis bulbi — end-stage shrunken, completely disorganised, fibrosed and calcified eyeball with severe hypotony.

Named in the instrument list (No. 43) for identification in the viva set. The transcribed notes give the name only, with no identification points or uses dictated — so nothing has been added beyond the source notes.

Named in the instrument list (No. 44) for identification. Related notes: Vannas scissors and De Wecker's scissors are used for anterior / open-sky vitrectomy when vitreous presents (vitreous loss in ICCE/ECCE or after a posterior capsular rent), and the pars-plana entries for vitrectomy are measured with the Castroviejo caliper — 4.0 mm behind the limbus in phakic eyes, 3.5 mm in pseudophakic eyes, 3.0 mm in aphakic eyes.

No. 11 blade: triangular blade. No. 15 blade: curved tip. Both fit the No. 3 Bard-Parker handle (see instrument 22) and are used for the ab-externo corneoscleral section, trabeculectomy, skin incisions (DCR, ptosis, lid surgery), dissecting the pterygium head, the chalazion incision and suture removal. Compare the blade breaker (instrument 23): razor-blade fragments are cheaper and sharper than both, but carbon steel rusts.

Named in the instrument list (No. 46) for identification in the viva set. The transcribed notes give the name only, with no identification points or uses dictated — so nothing has been added beyond the source notes.

t: 47 · Trial-Set Lenses — Pinhole, Concave, Convex & Cylindrical (identify)
b:
Pinhole: A black opaque disc with a small central aperture (1–1.5 mm). Principle — only the central paraxial rays pass straight through the nodal point without refraction, cutting off peripheral rays and increasing the depth of focus. Vision IMPROVES with the pinhole = refractive error (correctable up to about ±3 D; very high errors like −10 D, or aphakia +10 D, will not fully correct with a pinhole alone). Vision WORSENS = macular pathology (macular oedema, CSR, ARMD) or central media opacity (central corneal opacity, posterior subcapsular cataract).
Spherical concave (minus) lens — identification: forms a minified (smaller), erect, virtual image; on movement, the image moves WITH the lens; thin at the centre, thick at the periphery. Uses: correction of myopia; Hruby lens (−58.6 D), a planoconcave lens on the slit lamp for fundus biomicroscopy; the central lens of the Goldmann 3-mirror contact lens (−64 D) neutralises corneal refractive power.
Spherical convex (plus) lens — identification: magnified image when held close (inverted beyond its focal length); on movement, the image moves AGAINST the lens; thick at the centre, thin at the periphery. Uses: correction of hypermetropia, presbyopia and aphakia (high plus, about +10 D); +20 D condensing lens in indirect ophthalmoscopy; +90 D / +78 D non-contact lenses for slit-lamp fundus biomicroscopy; also used in the direct ophthalmoscope, retinoscope, synoptophore, slit lamp, operating microscope, keratometer and surgical loupes.
Cylindrical lens — identification: usually no handle, with two etched markings on the rim indicating the axis; there is NO power along the axis and maximum power perpendicular (90°) to it; moving the lens along the axis produces no image movement, moving it across the axis gives WITH movement (minus cylinder) or AGAINST movement (plus cylinder); rotating the lens causes a characteristic scissoring / optical swirling distortion. Use: correction of astigmatism (myopic or hypermetropic).
Named in the instrument list (No. 48) for identification in the trial set. The transcribed notes give the name only, so no uses have been added beyond the source notes.

Principle: Indentation tonometry — it measures how much a weighted plunger indents the anaesthetised cornea; a softer eye (low IOP) indents more, giving a HIGHER scale reading, and vice versa.
Components: Curved footplate, central plunger, holding bracket / handle, inclined scale with pointer, and detachable weights (5.5 g fixed on the plunger, plus 7.5 g, 10 g and 15 g additional weights).
Reading: The scale reading is converted into IOP (mmHg) using Friedenwald's conversion chart / table.

Identification: Long, angled blades with fine, sharp tips that meet precisely at the end, made to grasp the anterior lens capsule.
Use: Performing continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis (CCC) during cataract surgery — creating a smooth, tear-resistant circular opening in the anterior lens capsule. (Vannas scissors cover the alternative can-opener / envelope capsulotomy and cutting capsular tags.)

t: Video notes · Kelly's Descemet's Membrane Punch (Trabeculectomy Punch)
b:
Identification: A squeeze-action guillotine punch with a small cutting head at the tip.
Use: In trabeculectomy, it punches out a block of deep corneoscleral tissue (containing the trabecular meshwork and Schlemm's canal) beneath a partial-thickness superficial scleral flap. This creates a guarded fistula, allowing aqueous humour to drain from the anterior chamber into the subconjunctival space, forming a filtering bleb.

t: Video notes · Fixation Forceps (Lim's / Pierce Hoskins)
b:
Identification: Fine forceps with 1×2 teeth at the tip (Lim's, St. Martin's and Pierce Hoskins corneoscleral and conjunctival fixation forceps).
Uses: Holding and fixing the conjunctiva, Tenon's capsule or the scleral edge during peritomy, suturing and globe fixation.

Identification: A metallic handle with a round copper / brass ball and a pointed tip.
Use: Heated over a spirit lamp and applied to the bare sclera after peritomy to cauterise bleeding episcleral vessels (haemostasis) before making the scleral incision in cataract or glaucoma surgery.

t: Video notes · Schirmer's Tear Test Strip
b:
Material & dimensions: Whatman No. 41 filter paper, 5 mm wide × 35 mm long, with a fold / notch at 5 mm and a graduated millimetre scale (5 to 35 mm).
Procedure: The folded 5 mm end is hooked into the lower conjunctival fornix at the junction of the middle and lateral one-third of the lower eyelid (avoiding corneal contact) for 5 minutes.
Types: Without topical anaesthesia (Schirmer I) — measures total tear secretion (basal + reflex). With topical anaesthesia — measures basal secretion only.
Interpretation (wetting at 5 minutes): Normal — more than 15 mm (10–15 mm is borderline). Dry eye — less than 10 mm (less than 5 mm = severe dry eye).

Principle: A water-soluble orange-red dye (strip 1 mg / 2%) that fluoresces bright green when illuminated with the cobalt-blue filter on the slit lamp.
Uses: (1) Staining corneal epithelial defects, ulcers and abrasions — intact corneal epithelium is lipid-rich (hydrophobic) and repels fluorescein; where it is breached, the dye penetrates and stains the hydrophilic stroma bright green. (2) Goldmann applanation tonometry — it stains the tear film to form the two bright green semicircular mires of the doubling prism. (3) Seidel's test — detects aqueous leak from the anterior chamber (perforating injury, post-operative wound leak): leaking aqueous dilutes the dark orange dye into a bright green flowing stream. (4) Tear film break-up time (TBUT) — the time for the first dry black spot to appear in the green tear film after a blink; normal more than 10 seconds, less than 10 seconds is abnormal. (5) Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) — intravenous 5 ml of 10% (or 3 ml of 20%) fluorescein sodium into the antecubital vein with serial fundus photography, to evaluate retinal and choroidal vasculature in diabetic retinopathy, CRVO / BRVO, ARMD, neovascularisation and capillary non-perfusion.
